papers.summary: HPC facilities collect years of job scheduler records, yet much of this operational data remains underused because accessible tools for turning it into actionable insight are scarce. We present CQTwin, an open-source digital-twin toolkit for operational analytics of HPC scheduling data. CQTwin addresses this gap through two complementary modes: offline trace replay and online event-driven simulation. Built on the Python-based CQSim discrete-event simulator, CQTwin combines a fidelity-validated, high-performance C++ engine with an interactive browser-based dashboard and a Snapshot Lab, enabling facility staff, operators, and researchers to characterize workloads, compare scheduling policies, and explore what-if scenarios. As an offline twin, CQTwin replays archived workload traces under alternative policies to show how the same workload would have unfolded under different scheduling decisions. As an online twin, it consumes job events as they arrive and projects how alternative policies would process the currently queued jobs, providing guidance for real-time decision-making. The dashboard supports the complete analysis workflow, including workload characterization, experiment configuration and monitoring, and multidimensional comparison of simulation results, allowing users to determine visually which policies best suit a workload and what trade-offs they entail. We validate CQTwin using production traces from the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility spanning 2016-2023.

papers.title: FaaSpot: Fault-Tolerant Serverless Workflow Execution on Spot Instances
papers.summary: Serverless computing is increasingly used to run complex DAG workflows across diverse applications, and individual function execution times have grown to support them, pushing workflow makespans to hours. Open-source serverless platforms, deployed on a pool of VMs, typically use on-demand instances, and their cost increases with the makespan. Spot instances are far cheaper, but a preemption is likely before the workflow finishes. A preemption at a fan-out node or a task feeding a fan-in node stalls every parallel branch, cascading a single preemption into a workflow-wide failure. Prior systems address this challenge by migrating high-impact tasks to reliable, non-spot resources, sacrificing spot's cost advantage. We present FaaSpot, a serverless workflow execution system that runs every workflow task on spot instances with no on-demand fallback. Our key insight is that cascade-prone positions are determined by the DAG's topology and can be identified before execution. Therefore, FaaSpot analyzes the workflow DAG once at submission time and classifies each task by the impact of its preemption. Selective checkpointing, survival-aware scaling, and lineage-based retry then act on this single classification, with no runtime coordination. We evaluate FaaSpot on a trace-driven spot emulator with eight DAG workflows against four state-of-the-art baselines. FaaSpot completes 89.03% of runs at $0.018 per successful run, 21pp (percentage points) above the average baseline success rate and at a lower cost per success than every baseline, while reducing mean latency by 2.3x.

papers.title: Injection of Space Radiation Errors on Low-power NVM using Generative Deep Learning
papers.summary: We develop an error model for a Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) device that represents the effects of physical faults experienced in a CubeSat mission in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The CubeSat carries an off-the-shelf low-power Ferroelectric RAM (FRAM) chip and runs repeated read/write tests according to a predefined pattern. We compare every memory snapshot received from the satellite with a reference bitmap to identify bit errors. We visually analyze erroneous values distributions in the memory snapshots and we understand that they are frequently distributed according to regular spatial patterns. We define a generative deep learning technique to automatically learn these spatial patterns and to synthetically generate additional error patterns mimicking the observed ones. The model is capable at producing memory errors for general application-level experimentation. Our preliminary validation indicates that when comparing the model output with the data we collect, 0.92 of the generated bit flips correspond to bit flips in the memory snapshots and the model captures 0.91 of the observed bit flips. A comparison of the spatial distribution of bit flips in 10,000 generated error patterns also provides a Wasserstein distance of 0.073, indicating that the two distributions differ by roughly 7% of the maximum possible displacement of their probability masses.

papers.title: Client-Aware Security Adaptive Early Exit Vision Transformers for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) trains a shared model across data-owning clients without centralizing raw data, but client data difficulty and compute budgets can differ. We study local early-exit Vision Transformer (ViT) inference, where an intermediate classifier may return a prediction before the final Transformer stage. The proposed method replaces one global acceptance threshold with a client-specific base threshold from label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, then adjusts each input using predictive entropy, confidence, top-two class margin, and exit depth. Aggregation uses only clients that updated a parameter. Security-aware routing reaches 88.70% CIFAR-10 accuracy with 32.0% depth saving and 73.7% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 30\% saving. On matched six-client non-IID CIFAR-100, full-depth accuracy is 72.28% versus 68.20--71.80% for four heterogeneous-FL baselines; robustness-aware routing reaches 70.01% with 32.55% saving.

papers.title: Empirical Analysis of TEE-Enabled Rollup Designs
papers.summary: Layer 2 (L2) rollups have become the dominant scaling solution in Ethereum. At the core of these systems lies the rollup sequencer, a component that orders, executes, and submits L2 transaction blocks to the main Ethereum blockchain. The centralization of this sequencer introduces security risks, including censorship and malicious manipulation of transactions to extract maximum extractable value (MEV). Trusted execution environments (TEEs) provide strong hardware-enforced confidentiality and integrity guarantees for code and data. TEEs are strong candidates for strengthening security and ensuring verifiable neutrality in rollup sequencer operations, but multiple TEE-based designs are possible, offering different trade-offs among modularity, performance, and security guarantees. Among them, the separation of proposer and builder logic (PBS) into independent services is a strong contender against the monolithic approach that bundles all sequencer logic. Despite several proposed theoretical frameworks, there is a lack of experimental evaluation of the practicality and security trade-offs of integrating TEEs into rollup sequencers. This work addresses this gap through a comprehensive empirical study of TEE-enabled rollup designs under both PBS and monolithic sequencer models. Our experimental evaluations show that the impact of TEEs on rollup performance is small and that PBS does not significantly amplify it. We also show that PBS can lead to significant performance improvements by enabling more specialized, efficient builder logic implementations.

papers.title: Adding Heavy-Ball Momentum to Distributed Constrained Optimization for Energy Resource Management Subject to Time-Delays and Quantization
papers.summary: This paper studies a hybrid discrete-time signed gradient-consensus method with heavy-ball momentum, paired communication delays, and fixed logarithmic quantization. The method preserves the aggregate supply-demand equality at every iteration. For a static connected undirected graph and bounded delays, a Lyapunov-Krasovskii analysis establishes practical stability by isolating the discontinuous quantization error as an additive disturbance and closing a computable invariant-sublevel argument. The resulting ergodic residual bound is quadratic in the quantization resolution, and exact convergence to the smooth penalized equality-constrained optimizer is recovered in the unquantized case. For delay-free unquantized quadratic costs, an exact modal analysis identifies the heavy-ball stability region and optimal parameters, with the predicted rate validated on a fixed sparse network. A reproducible delayed experiment reports all constants and a certificate whose guaranteed steady-state level lies below the reported initialization. A separate mixed generator-battery experiment exercises the signed update directly. Finite smooth penalties approximate, but do not generally enforce, the local box constraints exactly.

papers.title: Low-Bit Distributed Constrained Optimization with Application to Optimal Scheduling and Allocation
papers.summary: This paper proposes a distributed resource allocation algorithm in which each agent communicates only the sign of its local cost gradient, a single bit per directed link per iteration. The algorithm is based on Laplacian-gradient dynamics and preserves the equality (demand) constraint at every iterate, guaranteeing anytime feasibility irrespective of termination time. First, we provide a complete Lyapunov-based convergence analysis for the fixed-step-size regime: the iterates are shown to enter, in at most O(1/\varepsilon^2) iterations, a neighborhood of the optimizer whose radius scales as O(\tau) in the decision variable and O(\tau^2) in the cost residual, where $\tau$ is the step-size. Crucially, the step-size bound is a time-invariant network constant (depending only on the graph Laplacian spectrum and the cost curvature bounds), so no adaptive tuning is required. Second, we characterize the invariant set under B-connected, weight-balanced digraphs, strictly weaker than the all-time connectivity and doubly-stochastic weights assumed in most prior work, and show that any odd, sign-preserving nonlinearity yields the same invariant-set and descent structure, with the single-bit protocol being the extreme communication-minimizing instance of a broader nonlinear class. Third, we address local box constraints via smooth penalty relaxation and quantify explicitly how the penalty weight interacts with the step-size bound and the optimality gap. Simulations on economic dispatch (1000 generators) and CPU scheduling (500 servers) demonstrate that the single-bit protocol achieves 5-60 times reduction in total communication cost relative to multi-bit baselines, at the price of a tunable and explicitly bounded optimality gap. A diminishing step-size schedule is shown empirically to eliminate this gap; its formal convergence analysis is identified as an open problem.

papers.title: SENTRY: A Streaming Edge Network Trust Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.summary: Real-time voice cloning has enabled large-scale streaming deepfake and vishing attacks, while existing Network Detection and Response (NDR) solutions rely on GPU-based post-processing that requires buffered audio and generalizes poorly to unseen speech synthesis models. This paper presents SENTRY, a hardware-oriented, streaming trust engine for inline deepfake detection at the network edge. SENTRY employs an integer lifting-wavelet front end together with a bank of multiplier-free transforms, including wavelet-packet envelopes, Walsh-Hadamard sequency profiles, waveform micro-statistics, and long-term spectral features, designed so that acoustic analysis needs only integer add, shift, compare and bitwise operations. A supervised gradient-boosted tree classifier is combined with an unsupervised Mahalanobis out-of-distribution detector trained solely on authentic speech, and their outputs are fused by a lightweight logistic layer to produce graduated LOG, CHALLENGE, or DROP actions. Under a closed-set protocol, SENTRY reaches 98.75% accuracy at a 1.25% equal-error rate (EER) on WaveFake, with perfect separation of HiFi-GAN and WaveGlow; its supervised track alone achieves an AUC of 0.9994 (fused: 0.9993). On ASVspoof 2019 LA (attacks A01-A06) over an 8 kHz mu-law telephony channel, it reaches 94.75% accuracy at a 5.05% EER, with a supervised-track AUC of 0.9948 (fused: 0.9884) and per-attack EERs below 7%. In our prototype, the feature front end runs as bit-exact integer code on one Arm Cortex-A53 core, and the classifier and fusion stage are synthesized for a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC using no DSP slices, returning a decision 220 ns after a feature vector is ready. These results indicate that deepfake screening can be placed inline without GPUs or floating-point hardware; generalization to unseen generators is left to future work.

papers.title: TideKV: Delayed KV Eviction via Layer-Wise Chunked Prefill for Memory-Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.summary: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is important for modern intelligent applications but remains constrained by peak memory during prompt prefill. Existing KV cache compression reduces decoding memory but typically requires full-prompt prefill to preserve global context, retaining a high construction peak. Online chunk-level eviction lowers memory earlier but selects before each layer has observed the complete prompt, potentially degrading cache construction and decoding. We present TideKV, an on-GPU cache-construction architecture using layer-major delayed eviction. TideKV processes all prompt chunks within each Transformer layer, retains full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at layer end. This schedule preserves full-prompt-aware selection while reducing activation and temporary memory. Experiments across multiple computing platforms show that TideKV preserves the inference quality and final cache size of the evaluated compression methods. At 64K on A100, it reduces the construction-time transient footprint by 83.89%. On RTX 4090, it increases time to first token by only 1.06% at 64K and enables 128K prefill. TideKV also completes 128K on Jetson, whereas matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory on both resource-constrained platforms. These results show that delayed layer-end eviction substantially expands feasible context lengths without sacrificing cache utility.

papers.title: Heart Signal (ECG) as Vibration Signature for Human Authentication Using TinyML
papers.summary: Ensuring data security in the era of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and deepfake technology requires robust biometric systems. Conventional methods such as facial recognition, iris scans, fingerprints, and voice recognition are increasingly vulnerable to spoofing and provide only one-time authentication at login. This study introduces an Electrocardiogram (ECG) based authentication framework, compared with Photoplethysmography (PPG), leveraging Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) for deployment on resource-constrained microcontroller units (MCUs). The proposed method enables continuous authentication, offering ongoing verification throughout device usage, which conventional biometrics cannot achieve. It also serves as a password-free solution, reducing risks of credential loss, theft, or reuse. However, ECG signals vary with physical activity, health conditions, age, and emotional states, requiring robust signal processing and learning algorithms. To address this, efficient TinyML models were designed to mitigate recognition errors from noisy real-time data. Experiments used single-lead ECG signals (Lead I) from UofTDB, MIT-BIH Arrhythmia, MIT-BIH Noise Stress Test, and PTB databases. Spectrograms and spectral features were extracted to train Deep Neural Network (DNN), 1D CNN, and 2D CNN models within the Edge Impulse platform, achieving 98% accuracy. The trained model was converted into TinyML format and deployed on an Espressif ESP-EYE (ESP32, 240 MHz). Support Vector Machine (SVM) models were also applied for benchmarking. By analyzing the number of heartbeats required for reliable recognition, the results show that averaging multiple signals improves tolerance to noise and enhances accuracy. Overall, ECG-based authentication demonstrates strong potential as a secure, real-time, and continuously verifiable method for personal identification on wearable and edge devices.

papers.title: From Trust Scores to Driver Decisions: An Abstaining Evidential Decision Layer for Event Validation in VANETs
papers.summary: Trust management in vehicular ad hoc networks is highly active, yet the decision that a driver needs, whether a reported event is real, has received far less attention; the schemes that make it force every decision into two outcomes, even on thin or conflicting evidence. This paper presents CREST, a vehicle-side event-decision framework that can withhold a decision its evidence does not support. Each vehicle weights the reports it holds by the trust, proximity and freshness of their senders, fuses them with Yager's rule, and decides only when the fused margin reaches an abstention threshold. Abstention is a waiting state: a vehicle still unsure at the event is resolved by an explicit application policy, which makes the trade-off between missed hazards and unnecessary detours visible. CREST requires only a scalar trust per reporter and is built here on an evidential trust model whose consensus and revocation steps are updated to support the decision layer. A single report is shown to change the decision margin by at most its weight, which bounds the influence of an attacker coalition by its trust. In a pre-registered simulation study with fourteen attacks, including position spoofing and trust-gated camouflage, and with all unspecified parameters of all systems tuned by the same procedure, CREST reduces the decision error of two published trust-based dissemination systems from 0.162 and 0.106 to 0.051. With the best-guess policy it also lowers both missed and unnecessary reroutes and outperforms the forced binary rule on both error types in every cell.

papers.title: Pattern-Driven Evaluation of LLM Code Optimization: Isolating Compiler-Transcendent Semantic Reasoning
papers.summary: Existing evaluations of LLM-based code optimization primarily measure end-to-end speedup, obscuring whether a model actually performs the intended optimization. For compiled languages, this is especially problematic: observed gains may reflect transformations already recoverable by modern optimizing compilers rather than optimization behavior attributable to the model itself. We present PatternBench, a benchmark for studying compiler-transcendent optimization, i.e., performance improvements that remain after aggressive compiler optimization. PatternBench targets residual optimization opportunities across seven classes of transformations and pairs runtime evaluation with an AST-based optimization faithfulness analysis that verifies whether the intended optimization is realized in the generated program. Experiments with frontier, open-weight, and fine-tuned models show that runtime speedup alone provides an incomplete account of optimization capability. Optimization faithfulness is strongly associated with realized speedup, and fine-tuning improves both faithfulness and optimization effectiveness. These results suggest that evaluation of LLM-based code optimization should measure not only performance outcomes, but also whether the target transformation was successfully executed.

papers.title: A general mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy
papers.summary: Foraging recruitment is a contagion: an agent finding a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade -- the model for rumour and adoption spread on social networks -- embedded in space. Because activation is degree-normalized, the same rule that spreads the cascade also stifles it as neighbourhoods crowd (density-dependent blocking), so the swarm aggregates on a resource, then releases to explore again. The cascade runs on the communication network, but acting on it moves agents in physical space, and that motion rewires the network: network and physical space are one coupled system, and this feedback -- not tuning -- makes the coordination self-limiting. Because recruitment chains along the graph rather than near neighbours alone, whether a discovery stays local or spans the swarm is a matter of percolation, and past a critical connectivity the swarm holds itself in a cascade window -- locally near-critical though globally subcritical, a self-organized, sandpile-like drive-avalanche cycle. Nothing is tuned, yet behaviours foraging biology documents separately emerge together -- recruitment, marginal-value patch-leaving, and Levy search with a switch to local exploitation. These are not coincidences but one least-committal principle: the resource field and the search both follow from maximum entropy -- Levy search matched to the field's sparsity, recruitment to its clustering, so active-matter order and optimal foraging are one system in two domains. The gains are real but conditional: up to 7.6x the harvest of solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, shrinking to nothing when search is already easy. Percolating cascades yield a large return on minimal communication. And that sparse, clustered field is the generic one -- resources almost inevitably aggregate, and maximum entropy makes it the least-committal one once they do -- so one untuned rule should recur widely.

papers.title: Conjugate Compilation: Self-Improving Agentic Co-Compilation for Speculative Decoding
papers.summary: As LLM adoption surges, scaling model serving requires unlocking stranded GPU capacity alongside deploying more GPUs. Speculative decoding brings two models into the serving process: a small draft model proposes tokens that a larger target model verifies. Yet compiling these models individually leaves their shared execution outside the compiler's optimization boundary. We introduce CONJUGATE COMPILATION, which reframes speculative decoding as a cross-model compilation problem and jointly optimizes the draft and target models within their shared execution rather than treating each in isolation. Our key insight is that cross-model compilation should be informed by the measured performance of the co-located shared execution it produces: an optimization that improves a kernel in isolation need not improve the models when they execute together. To expand cross-model opportunities, we devise operand layouts that interleave blocks from both models within common tiles, co-locating GEMM and non-GEMM work while preserving their mathematics. We realize CONJUGATE COMPILATION through a self-improving agentic search system in which an LLM edits cross-model optimization plans using the compiler and GPU execution as its environment. Each proposed plan is compiled and evaluated through its co-located shared execution, whose measured score, together with kernel-level verdicts and compiler feedback, informs subsequent proposals, while Monte Carlo tree search accumulates rewards to guide exploration. Across six single-GPU speculative-decoding configurations on NVIDIA B300 and RTX 5090 GPUs, CONJUGATE COMPILATION achieves a geometric-mean per-round speedup of 1.37x over conventional execution. Interleaved kernels raise this speedup to 1.45x, reaching 1.59x in the best case. CONJUGATE COMPILATION also improves GPU utilization on average by 1.46x on RTX 5090 and 1.50x on B300.

papers.title: DROD: Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout for Federated Continual Learning on Heterogeneous Devices
papers.summary: Federated learning for capacity-heterogeneous clients and federated continual learning are each well studied on their own, but their intersection -- clients holding differently sized models while every client's data stream also drifts over time -- remains underexplored. We study this setting directly, training a ResNet-18 fleet from scratch on Split-CIFAR-100 (10 tasks, class-incremental), and introduce DROD (Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout), which builds on FjORD's Ordered Dropout by using two independent reduction axes to extract sub-models: a shortcut ratio and a branch ratio. On a shared parameter/FLOP budget ladder, DROD achieves the highest mean accuracy among the heterogeneous-model federated learning strategies we compare. Its advantage over the two strongest baseline geometries persists across every replay-buffer size we test and under ER, DER++, and BiC; under EWC, all three geometries collapse alike.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Malware Image Classification under Data Heterogeneity
papers.summary: Malware image classification (MIC), in which binary files are converted into visual representations and deep neural networks are trained to identify malware families, has recently emerged as an effective approach for malware detection. Federated learning (FL) enables malware image classifiers to be trained collaboratively by multiple clients without sharing raw data. However, a fundamental challenge in FL is data heterogeneity (non-IID), which is particularly relevant but understudied in the malware context. In this paper, we address this gap via three contributions. First, we present an empirical study of federated MIC under varying degrees of data heterogeneity across three popular malware image datasets (MalImg, Virus-MNIST, and MalNet). We show that while FL achieves strong accuracy under IID conditions, both accuracy and training stability degrade as data becomes increasingly non-IID. Second, we introduce a set of round-level statistics that characterize the data contributed by participating clients in each FL round, and demonstrate that class entropy (diversity of class labels present in a given round) exhibits strong positive correlation with global model accuracy. Third, leveraging this insight, we propose an entropy-aware client selection strategy that filters candidate client subsets based on class entropy, and show that our strategy outperforms standard random selection. Our results highlight the role of client composition in federated MIC and underscore the importance of distribution-aware classifier training under data heterogeneity.

papers.title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
papers.summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.

papers.title: Peer-Relative Trust-Guided Update Screening for Robust Semi-Decentralized Federated Learning under Label-Flipping Attacks
papers.summary: Trust and reputation mechanisms can reduce the influence of malicious clients in federated learning (FL), but strict update filtering is difficult under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data because honest local updates may temporarily reduce performance on a shared validation proxy. Building on our earlier trust-based semi-decentralized FL (SDFL) framework, this paper operationalizes the trust signals and introduces peer-relative update screening that combines a robust validation-utility score with direction- and norm-based update quality. The method is evaluated with 50 MNIST clients, 20% persistent label-flip attackers, Dirichlet heterogeneity levels of 0.5 and 0.1, 100 communication rounds, and five paired random seeds. Under moderate heterogeneity, the proposed method reaches 98.37% final accuracy while rejecting 95.82% of malicious updates and retaining 90.30% of benign updates; the final benign and malicious trust distributions are completely separated (KS=1.00). Under severe heterogeneity, it reaches 95.25% accuracy, rejects 88.55% of malicious updates, and retains 76.90% of benign updates (KS=0.96). Trust weighting alone preserves slightly higher utility in the most heterogeneous condition, but accepts all malicious submis-sions. The results therefore distinguish influence mitigation from explicit containment and quantify the utility-selectivity trade-off introduced by screening. The study provides an empirically validated off-chain governance core that can feed blockchain-based audit and incentive layers in SDFL.

papers.title: Learn the Interface, Not the Implementation: Output Representation Dominates Training Regime in LLM-Based RTL Generation
papers.summary: Large-language-model register-transfer-level (RTL) generation has concentrated on how to train the model: fine-tuning, continued pre-training, and reinforcement learning from a verifier. We argue this is the second-order question. On a bounded, formally specifiable task of generating single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting (SECDED) ECC memory wrappers, we hold the task, data, and correctness oracle fixed and vary two axes independently: the training regime (seven settings) and the output representation (four levels, from fully expanded flat Verilog to an eight-field configuration expanded by a deterministic generator). Because a reference generator exists, correctness is decided by formal equivalence over a design space of approximately ten million points, rather than sampled from a hand-written testbench. Two results follow. First, representation dominates: every representation close to raw RTL reaches a pass rate of at most 0.17, while the configuration reaches 0.83 with no training at all. Once the model emits the configuration, every training regime achieves a pass rate between 0.89 and 1.00. Second, raw RTL hits a hard output-length limit: a 512-bit design requires 44,237 tokens of flat Verilog compared with just 69 tokens for the configuration. Consequently, raw generation becomes infeasible above 32-bit data words rather than merely inaccurate. A model trained from scratch with fewer than 50 million parameters, combined with the verified generator, achieves 0.89 formal equivalence, compared with 1.00 for a 32-billion-parameter fine-tuned model, while using approximately 1600 times less inference energy per correct design. Inference energy also dominates amortized training energy. The lesson is to learn the interface, not the implementation.

papers.title: A Dual-Uplink Dual-Satellite Architecture for Entanglement Distribution
papers.summary: Satellite-based quantum links are a promising enabler of long-distance entanglement distribution, overcoming the exponential losses of optical fibers. In uplink architectures, entangled photons are generated at ground stations and transmitted to orbiting satellites, reducing space-segment complexity but introducing significant atmospheric and geometric losses. Single-satellite dual-uplink configurations are additionally limited by the requirement of simultaneous visibility between both ground stations and the satellite. In this work, we investigate a dual-uplink dual-satellite network architecture and compare its performance with the single-satellite scheme under identical physical assumptions. The proposed topology introduces an inter-satellite link (ISL) that decouples the ground-station separation from the atmospheric uplink geometry. A realistic channel model is employed, incorporating geometric attenuation, atmospheric turbulence, background noise, and Bell-state measurement efficiency. The overall success probability and practical fidelity are evaluated as functions of satellite altitude and ground-station separation. Our results show that while the single-satellite configuration is suitable for regional-scale networks, it becomes infeasible for large separations due to geometric constraints. The proposed dual-satellite architecture mitigates this limitation and significantly extends the achievable communication distance, representing a key step toward scalable quantum internet infrastructures.

papers.title: Superposed analog memory for vector storage in neural networks
papers.summary: The growing memory demands of artificial neural networks pose a major challenge for energy-efficient computing, particularly for models that rely on large collections of high-dimensional weight and embedding vectors. Conventional memory architectures store these vectors individually, requiring many memory cells per vector and limiting achievable storage density. Here we demonstrate an analog memory architecture that encodes multiple vectors in a distributed superposition within a single memory array. Individual vectors are recovered through in-memory matrix-vector multiplication, allowing the degree of superposition to be tuned to balance storage density against recall fidelity. This approach introduces a new scaling dimension for analog memory, in which effective storage density can be increased without a corresponding increase in the number of physical memory cells. The distributed representation also provides resilience to device-level noise. We implement the architecture on a prototype phase-change memory chip and experimentally evaluate it using embedding tables from deep learning recommendation models and large language models. The results demonstrate inference accuracy comparable to full-precision software baselines, establishing analog superposition as a promising route towards dense, energy-efficient memory for artificial intelligence.

papers.title: K-AoI: A Spatio-Temporal Synchronization Metric for Digital Twin-based Teleoperation in Dynamic Network Environments
papers.summary: Synchronization between a digital twin (DT) and its physical robot is critical for effective teleoperation, as mismatches directly degrade operator awareness and task performance. Existing synchronization metrics are predominantly time-based and rarely capture the spatial consequences of delayed information during motion. In this paper, we introduce Kinematic Age of Information (K-AoI), a spatio-temporal metric that weights AoI by instantaneous Cartesian velocity, translating temporal staleness into physically meaningful spatial divergence. We implement and evaluate K-AoI on a DT teleoperation testbed comprising a six-degrees-of-freedom (6-DOF) manipulator, a Unity-based twin, and controlled network impairments using tc netem across seven network conditions. Per-sample analysis shows that K-AoI exhibits rank-correlations with AoI at $\rho \leq 0.65$ across all networks, dropping to $\rho = 0.22$ under satellite connections. This shows that K-AoI is not a simple transformation of AoI, but instead captures velocity-dependent degradation effects that time-only metrics cannot resolve. We further analyze AoI tail behavior using Ultra-Low AoI (ULAoI) and find that the commonly assumed Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) model is rejected. This reflects the impact of deterministic forwarding and bounded jitter, which violate standard extreme-value assumptions. Overall, K-AoI provides a complementary and physically grounded synchronization metric, linking network delay to task-relevant spatial error in digital-twin teleoperation systems. The dataset and testbed software are publicly available at: https://github.com/luziyaotian/kaoi-testbed.

papers.title: Bidirectionality is Necessary in Cellular Machines for Exact-Arrival Multi-Agent Path Finding
papers.summary: On ranked directed acyclic graphs coupled by vertex conflicts we study exact-arrival multi-agent path finding (departure and arrival pinned in place and time) posed as a distributed output task: every cell must emit its own bit of a valid joint path-support mask. The machines are cellular: one automaton per cell, state factored over cells, communication only along a fixed local fabric, synchronous rounds, a query-independent output round, no central decoder, and a per-topology transition code. "Necessary" here means: on an explicit hard topology, over all its feasible queries, no universally correct local-only architecture can renounce either temporal orientation; with global flags, impossibility becomes a bandwidth-round trade-off. The class is not vacuous: a flooding machine solves every instance in as many rounds as the diameter of the local fabric. The bound survives two concessions: we supply every agent's exact individual cavity, which alone solves the single-agent problem in zero rounds and makes the single-agent direction theorem vacuous; and we allow $k$ one-bit global aggregate flags. On a twelve-cell, two-agent, depth-three topology no forward-only machine with $k=0$ is correct on two feasible queries, for any number of rounds; the time-reversed topology does the same to backward-only machines. Placing $p$ copies side by side gives, for forward-only machines, $J_R+kR\ge p$ at constant depth, where $J_R$ measures how much of the query reaches the targets' cones and is $0$ here. A backward-only machine solves that family in constant rounds and a flag-streaming one in $\lceil p/k\rceil+O(1)$, so the bound is tight in order; on the composite family neither orientation can be renounced. The finite lemmas of the gadget and the pair-invariance contradictions are checked in Lean 4; the semantic bridge, the cone lemma and the counting are paper proofs. We report no benchmarks.

papers.title: A Generic On-Board AI Processing Chain for Earth Observation: From Application Development to Embedded Deployment and Mission-Level Orchestration
papers.summary: Earth observation satellites acquire more data than they can downlink. Extracting information on board with artificial intelligence (AI) turns the satellite into a data-reduction stage that downlinks compact products, such as masks or detections, instead of full scenes; deploying it in a mission, however, involves the whole processing chain and not only the neural network. We present a generic on-board AI processing chain along three axes, with wildfire segmentation as the worked example among ship detection and cloud segmentation. (i) The AI model is tuned (spectral-band selection, input normalization), quantized to 8-bit integers (int8) and ported to an AMD Versal VCK190, with its excellent segmentation performance preserved on the board. (ii) A modular tiler-inference-mosaicer workflow, reused unchanged across applications, brings the tile-level model to scene level, turning a full acquisition into a scene-level mask or detection list. (iii) Each step is packaged as a unikernel and orchestrated on board by ORCHIDE, a cloud-native orchestrator. The chain is characterized end to end, from the standalone execution on the target to its execution under orchestration with parallel workflows on a representative test bench. Beyond AI inference on individual tiles, this approach aims at increasing the maturity of on-board AI deployment by addressing a complete processing chain, from the acquired scene to the mission-level execution.

papers.title: Connection Escrow: Holding AI-Agent Pod Egress in the Kernel Until an Isolated Verifier Rules
papers.summary: AI agents in containers act by opening network connections, and the text that drives them can be hostile. Controls placed between the agent and its tools are bypassed by a child process or a direct socket, and their approval is not tied to the connection the kernel later opens. We present connection escrow: every outbound TCP connection from a supervised pod is parked inside the kernel's connect() path, before any packet exists, by a 98-instruction eBPF program on the pod's cgroup. A node interceptor attributes the held socket to its kernel socket cookie, process, executable digest, cgroup and pod identity, parks the first bytes the agent writes, and asks a verifier in a separate container with its own key. The connection is released only on a signed verdict naming that one socket cookie and destination, unexpired and unused; no verdict by the deadline resets it, and a late approval is refused. The agent is unmodified. A 36-check adversarial suite with real cgroups passes on the eBPF hold point (33 of the checks also apply, and pass, on an iptables hold point): refused connections never reach the destination; forged, rebound, replayed, expired and late verdicts are refused; the agent's attempt to reach the verifier is itself escrowed; child-process and renamed-binary bypasses fail; UDP is pinned to the resolver. On a Kubernetes cluster, unmodified pods are held per connection and attributed to their SPIFFE identity, a raw socket that bypasses a sidecar proxy is held, and 600 connections from six pods are gated. The hold adds 4.5 ms median per released connection, of which 24 us is policy. Finally, we gate on request content without terminating TLS: an eBPF uprobe reads the plaintext at the agent's TLS-library boundary (shared OpenSSL, static OpenSSL, Go crypto/tls), a model scores it, and the connection is held on that verdict while TLS stays end-to-end and the enforcer holds no key.

papers.title: GeoSplit: Selective Edge--Server Map Acquisition for Cross-User Travel-Mode Recognition
papers.summary: Networked mobility sensing couples local trajectory inference with remote geospatial context, making communication decisions part of the prediction system. We present GeoSplit, an edge--server framework for travel-mode recognition that separates the utility of map evidence, its training-time transfer, and its selective acquisition at runtime. On GeoLife with 10% labels, we evaluate these components under user-day and user-disjoint grouping. For unseen users, aligned full-map context raises macro-F1 from 0.7154 to 0.7864, while map-informed distillation yields a motion-only student at 0.7225. Through a compact query interface, entropy gating achieves 0.7729 macro-F1 versus 0.7738 for all queries, querying 39.5% of trajectories and reducing application payload by 60.5%. Under user-day grouping, selective and all-query scores are similarly close at a 21.6% query rate. Learned value estimation and probability fusion offer no consistent improvement. These results illustrate communication-efficient edge--server inference for an intelligent transportation sensing task.

papers.title: DaPPA: A Unified Data-Parallel Programming Framework for Efficient Processing-in-Memory Execution
papers.summary: Processing-in-memory (PIM) alleviates data-movement bottlenecks by placing computation near or inside memory. Two general-purpose PIM paradigms are now practical: processing-near-memory (PNM) and processing-using-memory (PUM). Although both target regular, data-intensive, data-parallel workloads, they remain difficult to program because data organization is tightly coupled to computation and differs across substrates. Thus, programmers must manually manage substrate-specific data partitioning, movement, layout, and tiling, preventing program portability across PIM systems. We propose DaPPA (data-parallel processing-in-memory architecture), a programming framework that exposes a single high-level data-parallel pattern interface and retargets it to multiple PIM substrates. The key idea of DaPPA is to decouple the expression of data parallelism from substrate-specific data organization: programmers express computation once using data-parallel patterns and a dataflow interface, while specialized backends automatically generate data orchestration for PNM and multi-level tiling for PUM. We evaluate DaPPA on representative substrates from both PIM paradigms. On the UPMEM PNM system, DaPPA outperforms hand-tuned implementations by 1.6x on average with 95% fewer lines-of-code, and outperforms the state-of-the-art SimplePIM framework by 1.4x on average with 62% fewer lines-of-code. On a SIMDRAM-like PUM substrate, DaPPA outperforms the state-of-the-art MIMDRAM compiler by 2.0x on average (up to 6.4x) across 12 workloads. DaPPA can deploy all ten of our PNM workloads, whereas CINM, the closest framework targeting both paradigms, can deploy only three, on which DaPPA is 2.7--6.8x faster. We open-source DaPPA at https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/DaPPA.

papers.title: Fine-Grained Parallel Graph Algorithms Can Be Both Fast and Scalable
papers.summary: Making graph algorithms fast and scalable on traditional architectures and GPUs often involves breaking them into large, coarse-grained computational blocks that access similar regions of memory. We show that graph algorithms, which have tremendous vertex- and edge-level parallelism, can be scaled as fine-grained programs on suitable architectures. Specifically, we investigate graph algorithms on the UpDown architecture and show how this many-threaded, cache-less architecture enables simple, fine-grained parallel graph algorithms to be both fast and scalable. Single-node UpDown performance is 28x (geomean) over an H200 GPU, and that same program scales to 1000's of nodes. We evaluate the system three ways: simulation, analytical projection models, and selected validation studies at scale (simulation of 16,384 UpDown nodes, using 256 supercomputer nodes). These results show the UpDown system can achieve 680K giga-traversed edges per second (GTEPS) for PageRank and 989K GTEPS BFS, exceeding prior results significantly.

papers.title: CrossTL: Hub-Based Translation of GPU Programs and the Preservation of Source Rules
papers.summary: GPU programs are written in vendor languages that disagree about integer overflow, division by zero, NaN handling, floating-point contraction, data layout and dispatch, so a translated program can compile and still compute something else. We describe CrossTL, an open-source translator that routes ten GPU source languages to eleven targets through CrossGL, a textual hub language, with repository-scale porting, contracts that loaders check, and native parity tests. We define faithful translation as refinement up to rejection under a compile configuration, and test whether a hub that records each source rule and lowers it through one per-target table keeps rules that a syntax-only hub loses. On an internally pre-registered suite of 66 hazard kernels in six languages, run on an Apple GPU through Metal, MoltenVK and WebGPU and on CPU implementations of Vulkan, OpenGL and an emulated Direct3D 12, SPIRV-Cross, naga, Tint, Slang and CrossTL each lose some source rule, and outcomes change with Metal's math mode and between two Vulkan implementations. A rule-carrying prototype of the hub removes 34 of 39 divergences on the rules it carries, against 14 for local fixes to four SPIR-V defects, and refuses where WGSL cannot express a rule. The registered hypothesis that it keeps every rule fails: MoltenVK, a non-conformant Vulkan layer, drops a rule that correct SPIR-V carries natively. On 2,585 programs written by third parties, 31% of CrossTL's translations are usable, established translators produce valid output significantly more often in 31 of 39 comparisons, and carrying the rules changes no target's accepted share by more than 0.2 points. Recording each operation's source rule suffices for the rules tested but is not necessary: one strongest rule would keep them too, at about nine times as many rewrites and 58 more refusals on the corpus.

papers.title: VeriGRAG: Enhancing LLM-Based Verilog Code Generation with Structure-Aware Soft Prompts
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generating Verilog code from natural language descriptions. However, Verilog code inherently encodes the structural characteristics of hardware circuits, including data path organization and interconnections among components. Effectively leveraging these structural characteristics to enhance the functional and syntactic correctness of LLM-based Verilog code generation remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, we propose VeriGRAG, a novel framework that converts Verilog code into data path graphs and employs graph neural networks (GNNs) to encode their structural information. A multimodal retriever, trained through knowledge distillation from a cross-attention encoder to a dual encoder, then selects the graph embeddings most relevant to the input hardware description. The VeriFormer module uses learnable query tokens and two-stage training to extract code-relevant structural features and align them with the LLM's input embedding space, producing structure-aware soft prompts. Experiments on VerilogEval and RTLLM show improvements in both syntactic and functional correctness. With Qwen2.5-Coder-32B as its backbone, VeriGRAG achieves the highest functional $pass@1$ and $pass@5$ scores among the compared methods on both benchmarks.

papers.title: Decentralized Decoding with Adaptive Local Combining for Cell-Free Massive MIMO
papers.summary: In existing literature, a two-stage architecture comprising of large-scale fading decoding (LSFD) at the central processing unit (CPU) and local combining at the access points (APs) is commonly deployed for uplink processing in scalable cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-mMIMO) systems. However, centralized LSFD (c-LSFD) requires cross-AP channel statistics at the CPU and local combining uses schemes that either do not suppress interference optimally or result in analytically intractable solutions. We provide novel schemes to address both concerns. First, we propose the decentralized LSFD (d-LSFD) scheme that maximizes a surrogate signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio built only from local interference covariance statistics and identify covariance-action regime where it is equivalent to c-LSFD. Second, based on the fact that the antennas at each AP provide spatial degrees of freedom (DoFs) for both interference suppression and coherent array gain, we interpret every combining scheme as solving the optimal DoF allocation problem over available DoFs. Selective zero-forcing (ZF) schemes solve this problem over both the dimension and composition of the local ZF subspace. We then provide the DoF-adaptive ZF-subspace (DAZS) combining scheme, which lets each AP select the optimal directions in the ZF subspace by maximizing its local sum spectral efficiency. Our numerical results establish the efficacy and efficiency of the proposed schemes compared to the corresponding existing schemes.

papers.title: Hardware-Efficient Accurate 4-bit Multiplier for Xilinx 7 Series FPGAs
papers.summary: As IoT and edge inference proliferate, there is a growing need for lookup-table (LUT)-based multipliers that combine a low LUT count with a high maximum operating frequency. This paper proposes a hardware-efficient exact unsigned 4 x 4-bit multiplier for AMD Xilinx 7-series FPGAs. By reorganizing the logic functions mapped to the LUTs, the proposed design uses 11 LUTs and two CARRY4 blocks and achieves a maximum operating frequency of 361.402 MHz. Among the eight evaluated configurations, it has the lowest LUT count and the secondhighest maximum operating frequency.

papers.title: Instrumentation Optimization for Practical Dynamic Race Detection
papers.summary: Dynamic data race detectors are successful at flagging concurrency bugs, but their high runtime overhead limits adoption. This overhead stems primarily from pervasive instrumentation of memory accesses -- a significant fraction of which is for safe accesses. We address this inefficiency through a compiler-integrated approach that identifies safe accesses using static analysis and eliminates instrumentation for these. We strike a careful balance between analysis precision and cost, to ensure applicability to real-world applications. We show that our optimizations never cause ThreadSanitizer to miss races it would otherwise detect. We further observe that many checks are redundant: They only flag a race if a preceding check has already flagged an equivalent race for the same memory location. We show that, when reporting one representative per class is sufficient, even more instrumentation can be eliminated. Lastly, we introduce a dynamic technique that skips instrumentation when there is only one thread at runtime, even when this could not be determined statically. We integrate these static analyses and program transformations into the ThreadSanitizer race detector based on LLVM. Our experiments on a diverse suite of real-world applications, including Memcached, Redis, SQLite, MySQL, and Chromium, demonstrate that our optimizations reduce the number of instrumentation calls at runtime by up to 91% and yield application-level speedups of up to 1.91x, a geometric-mean Chromium speedup of 1.25x on Blink and 1.14x on Speedometer 3.0, and peak speedups reaching 2.28x on Memcached with two server threads. Our optimizations are in the process of being upstreamed into ThreadSanitizer.

papers.title: SparsePixels: Efficient Convolution for Sparse Data on FPGAs
papers.summary: Inference of standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on FPGAs often incurs high latency and a long initiation interval due to the deep nested loops required to densely convolve every input pixel regardless of its feature value. However, input features can be spatially sparse in some image data, where semantic information may occupy only a small fraction of the pixels and most computation would be wasted on empty regions. In this work, we introduce SparsePixels, a framework that implements sparse convolution on FPGAs by selectively retaining and computing on a small subset of active input pixels while ignoring the rest, reducing the per-layer compute from $O(HWK^2C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}})$ to $O(n^2C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}})$ and the storage from $O(HWC)$ to $O(nC)$ when $n^2\ll HW$. Because computation always runs over a single pre-specified pixel budget that is frozen at synthesis, the inference latency is data-independent and constant at runtime. We show that, for identifying neutrino interactions in naturally sparse LArTPC images with 4k pixels, a standard CNN with a compact size of 4k parameters incurs an inference latency of 48.665 $\mu$s on an FPGA, whereas a sparse CNN of the same base architecture, computing on less than 1% of the input pixels, achieves a $\times 73$ speedup to 0.665 $\mu$s with resource utilization well within on-chip budgets, trading only a small percent-level performance loss. This work aims to benefit future algorithm development for efficient data readout in modern experiments with strict latency requirements of microseconds or below.

papers.title: FairShare: Auditable Geographic Fairness for Multi-Operator LEO Spectrum Sharing
papers.summary: Dynamic spectrum sharing (DSS) among multi-operator low Earth orbit (LEO) mega-constellations is essential for coexistence, yet prevailing policies focus almost exclusively on interference mitigation, leaving geographic equity largely unaddressed. This work investigates whether conventional DSS approaches inadvertently exacerbate the rural digital divide. Incorporating Keplerian orbital dynamics, inter-beam co-channel interference, and three real-world constellation geometries (Starlink, OneWeb, Kuiper), we conduct large-scale, 3GPP-compliant non-terrestrial network (NTN) simulations across 20 orbital snapshots spanning 10~minutes of satellite motion. The results uncover a stark and persistent structural bias: SNR-priority scheduling induces a $1.84\times$ mean urban--rural access disparity, with temporal fluctuations reaching $3.9\times$ during favorable interference conditions. Counter-intuitively, increasing system bandwidth amplifies rather than alleviates this gap. To remedy this, we propose FairShare, a lightweight, quota-based framework that enforces geographic fairness. FairShare not only reverses the bias, achieving an affirmative disparity ratio of $\Delta_{\text{geo}} = 0.68\times$ with zero variance across all orbital snapshots and interference conditions, but also reduces scheduler runtime by 3.3\%. This demonstrates that algorithmic fairness can be achieved without trading off efficiency or complexity, and that it remains invariant to physical-layer dynamics. Our work provides regulators with both a diagnostic metric for auditing fairness and a practical, enforceable mechanism for equitable spectrum governance in next-generation satellite networks.

papers.title: Load Balancing with Evolving Workloads in Large-Scale Language Model Serving
papers.summary: Serving large language models requires assigning requests whose workloads grow during processing and whose completion times are unknown. With a synchronization barrier, lightly loaded workers wait for the slowest worker at every decode iteration. We model this loss through aggregate workload imbalance and formulate a joint admission and assignment problem with sticky requests and capacity limits. Short lookahead incorporates predicted completions of ongoing requests. For exact optimization without lookahead, we prove a comparison under independent geometric decode lengths, bounded independent nondegenerate prompt sizes, and batched releases satisfying a cumulative supply condition. The long-run expected imbalance improvement over first come, first served admission with request-count join-shortest-queue grows at least as the square root of the product of worker capacity and the logarithm of worker count, in the stated scaling regime. The comparison extends to capacity-aware round robin, random routing, and power of two choices. BalanceRoute approximations connect the formulation to practical routing. Experiments using up to 144 NPUs with proprietary and public traces show lower workload spread and higher throughput than the evaluated baselines. These empirical results complement the guarantee for exact optimization.

papers.title: Do We Need Asynchronous SGD? On the Near-Optimality of Synchronous Methods
papers.summary: Modern distributed optimization methods mostly rely on traditional synchronous approaches, despite substantial recent progress in asynchronous optimization. We revisit Synchronous SGD and its robust variant, called $m$-Synchronous SGD, which can be interpreted as a method with a backup-worker strategy, and theoretically show that they are nearly optimal in many heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios, which is somewhat unexpected. We analyze the synchronous methods under random times and adversarial partial participation of workers, and prove that their time complexities are optimal in many practical regimes, up to logarithmic factors. While synchronous methods are not universal solutions and there exist tasks where asynchronous methods may be necessary, we show theoretically that they are sufficient for many modern heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios.

papers.title: GRAU: A Generic Runtime-Reconfigurable Activation-Requantization Unit for Quantized Neural Network Accelerators
papers.summary: As neural networks continue to scale, low-precision quantization is widely adopted in edge accelerators, but conventional multi-threshold activation hardware requires 2^n-1 thresholds for n-bit integer outputs, leading to rapidly increasing hardware costs. We propose GRAU, a Generic Runtime-Reconfigurable Activation-Requantization Unit that fuses batch normalization, nonlinear activation, and requantization through piecewise-linear fitting with Power-of-Two slopes. GRAU requires only basic comparators and 1-bit right shifters, while supporting mixed-precision quantization and runtime switching among post-accumulation functions, including modern nonlinear activations such as SiLU and GELU. Compared with multi-threshold activation-requantization units, GRAU reduces LUT consumption by approximately 90% or more while improving hardware efficiency, flexibility, and scalability. We further explore the trade-off between accuracy and hardware cost across different approximation settings and provide an open-source toolchain for GRAU-aware network training.

papers.title: SliceMapper: Intelligent Mapping of O-CU and O-DU onto O-Cloud Sites in 6G O-RAN
papers.summary: In this paper, we propose an rApp, named SliceMapper, to optimize the mapping process of the open centralized unit (O-CU) and open distributed unit (O-DU) of an open radio access network (O-RAN) slice subnet onto the underlying open cloud (O-Cloud) sites in sixth-generation (6G) O-RAN. To accomplish this, we first design a system model for SliceMapper and introduce its mathematical framework. Next, we formulate the mapping process addressed by SliceMapper as a sequential decision-making optimization problem. To solve this problem, we implement both on-policy and off-policy variants of the Q-learning algorithm, employing tabular representation as well as function approximation methods for each variant. To evaluate the effectiveness of these approaches, we conduct a series of simulations under various scenarios. We proceed further by performing a comparative analysis of all four variants. The results demonstrate that the on-policy function approximation method outperforms the alternative approaches in terms of stability and lower standard deviation across all random seeds. However, the on-policy and off-policy tabular representation methods achieve higher average rewards, with values of 5.42 and 5.12, respectively. Finally, we conclude the paper and introduce several directions for future research.

papers.title: Partitioning Unstructured Sparse Tensor Algebra for Load-Balanced Parallel Execution
papers.summary: Sparse tensor algebra is challenging to efficiently parallelize due to the irregular, data-dependent, and potentially skewed structure of sparse computation. We propose the first partitioning algorithm that provably load balances the computation of any sparse tensor algebra expression across parallel execution units. Our algorithm generalizes parallel merging algorithms to any number of operands, and to multi-dimensional, hierarchical sparse data structures. We implement our algorithm within an existing sparse tensor algebra compilation framework to automatically generate parallel sparse tensor algebra kernels that target multi-core CPUs and GPUs. We show that our generated code is competitive with hand-implemented parallelization strategies used by vendor libraries like Intel MKL and NVIDIA cuSPARSE (geo-means of $0.93$--$5.5\times$) and \taco (geo-means of $1.2$--$2.4\times$), and significantly outperforms PyTorch Sparse's general-purpose strategies on sparse tensor expressions where specialized algorithms have not been developed (geo-means of $2.0$--$9.1\times$).

papers.title: Exposing Embedded Matrix Multiplication with polyhedral transformations for CGRA compilation
papers.summary: Matrix-matrix multiplication (mmul) is a dominant computing pattern in edge workloads, but in real applications it is often embedded within larger affine programs and intertwined with other operations. Coarse-Grained Reconfigurable Arrays (CGRAs) can flexibly and efficiently support it, since they combine operation-level reconfigurability and high energy efficiency. However, mapping computational kernels that include mmul with state-of-the-art compilation strategies often leads to suboptimal results, since its multi-dimensional structure hampers the uncovering of its inherent parallelism and, ultimately, runtime performance. This paper presents Kernel-CGRA, a compiler flow that uses polyhedral transformations to expose legal affine mmul subspaces, lower each accepted region to a back-end-independent operation, and preserve the surrounding computation in the generic CDFG path. For CGRA execution, the operation is instantiated as a parametric output-stationary kernel, while residual regions are reconnected through context generation and live-value preservation. The matcher is intentionally strict: only regions proven to match the supported affine mmul form are rewritten. Across canonical, fused, and application-level benchmarks, Kernel-CGRA achieves runtime speedups of up to 10.2x over state-of-the-art CGRA CDFG compilation with modulo scheduling and loop unrolling.

papers.title: Efficient Training on Multiple Consumer GPUs with RoundPipe
papers.summary: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on consumer-grade GPUs is highly cost-effective, yet constrained by limited GPU memory and slow PCIe interconnects. Pipeline parallelism combined with CPU offloading mitigates these hardware bottlenecks by reducing communication overhead. However, existing PP schedules suffer from an inherent limitation termed the \textit{weight binding} issue. Binding uneven model stages (e.g., the LM head is large) to GPUs limits the pipeline's throughput to that of the GPU with the heaviest load, leading to severe pipeline bubbles. In this paper, we propose RoundPipe, a novel pipeline schedule that breaks the weight binding constraint on consumer GPU servers. RoundPipe treats GPUs as a pool of stateless execution workers and dynamically dispatches computation stages across devices in a round-robin manner, achieving a near-zero-bubble pipeline. To ensure training correctness and system efficiency, RoundPipe integrates a priority-aware transfer scheduling engine, a Layerwise Model Consistency Protocol, and an automated layer partitioning algorithm. Evaluations on an 8$\times$ RTX 4090 server demonstrate that RoundPipe achieves 1.48--2.16$\times$ speedups over state-of-the-art baselines when fine-tuning 1.7B to 32B models. Remarkably, RoundPipe enables LoRA fine-tuning of the Qwen3-235B model with 31K sequence length on a single server. RoundPipe has been open-sourced as a Python library.

papers.title: Coral: Cost-Efficient Multi-LLM Serving over Heterogeneous Cloud GPUs
papers.summary: The landscape of large language models (LLMs) has become increasingly fragmented, with no single model dominating the field. Meanwhile, cloud providers offer a diverse array of mid-tier and older-generation GPUs. These heterogeneous resources provide better availability and deliver comparable performance-per-dollar to top-tier hardware. To efficiently harness these GPUs for concurrent multi-LLM serving, we introduce Coral: an adaptive, heterogeneity-aware serving system. The key idea behind Coral is the joint optimization of resource allocation and replica serving strategies across all models. To keep pace with shifting throughput demands and resource availability, Coral employs a lossless, two-stage decomposition. This approach preserves joint optimality while reducing online solve times from hours to mere tens of seconds. Evaluations across 6 models and 20 GPU configurations demonstrate that Coral reduces serving costs by up to 2.79$\times$ compared to the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 2.39$\times$ higher goodput under scarce resource constraints.

papers.title: SIGMA: A Versatile Streaming Graph Partitioner for Vertex- and Edge-Balanced Distributed GNN Training
papers.summary: Distributed Graph Neural Network (GNN) training depends critically on how the underlying graph is partitioned across compute resources. Existing graph partitioners focus either on vertex partitioning or edge partitioning and typically optimize only a single communication objective (edge cut vertex cut) under a single balance constraint (vertex balance edge balance). We present SIGMA (Streaming Integrated Graph Partitioning with Multi-objective Awareness), a versatile streaming graph partitioner that supports both vertex and edge partitioning within a unified multi-objective, multi-constraint framework. Depending on the target distributed GNN system, SIGMA can be configured for edge-cut-oriented vertex partitioning or vertex-cut-oriented edge partitioning while simultaneously accounting for vertex and edge balancing. A clustering-based preprocessing stage incorporates global graph structure to improve partition quality while preserving the efficiency and scalability advantages of streaming partitioning. We evaluate SIGMA on six benchmark graphs spanning diverse domains and scales using two distributed GNN training systems: DistGNN (edge-partitioned) and DistDGL (vertex-partitioned). Across both settings, SIGMA consistently achieves strong performance, showing its ability to navigate complex trade-offs between partition quality, training efficiency, and memory consumption, frequently outperforming established streaming approaches and delivering competitive results against high-quality in-memory partitioners, with particularly strong results in edge-partitioned GNN training. These results demonstrate that a unified streaming partitioner can effectively address the communication, compute, and memory challenges of distributed GNN training across fundamentally different system architectures.

papers.title: CHERI-D: Secure and efficient inline object ID for CHERI temporal memory safety
papers.summary: We propose CHERI-D, an architectural extension to CHERI that supports efficient temporal memory safety. Efficient memory safety is an increasing priority for programming languages, operating systems, and hardware designs, and CHERI is a leading hardware/software system that provides native spatial safety and a foundation for temporal memory safety. Due to CHERI lacking intrinsic architectural support for temporal memory safety, the state-of-the-art CHERI temporal safety solution, Cornucopia Reloaded, is a software-based solution that provides use-after-reallocation (UAR) protections instead of the stronger use-after-free (UAF) mitigation, and suffers performance overhead due to delayed reallocation and revocation. CHERI-D associates object identification (ID) metadata with capability pointers to provide temporal integrity of allocations. CHERI spatial safety allows CHERI-D to store object IDs safely inline with allocation data, potentially within unused fragmentation. Evaluated in simulation and in hardware, CHERI-D significantly reduces the revocation overhead of Cornucopia Reloaded while allowing it to support strict use-after-free mitigation.

papers.title: Cyclic Graphs and Memoization in Pure $\lambda$-Calculus
papers.summary: Purely functional programming makes immutability and non-strict evaluation its defaults; we push further, making interning and memoization the defaults of computation. In prior operational semantics for the pure $\lambda$-calculus, representing and transforming cyclic and infinite data requires an added recursion construct, a $\texttt{letrec}$, a $\mu$-binder, or a built-in $Y$ for graph reduction, and sharing the repeated work of a memoized or dynamic-programming function requires an impure cache. We show that no extension is needed. We apply tabling, the standard method for solving a least-fixpoint equation, to weak-head reduction; this defines a new operational semantics for the pure $\lambda$-calculus that keeps each term's standard lazy meaning. A term that reaches finitely many distinct states, each solved in finitely many steps, comes out as a finite graph, possibly cyclic; the calculus stays pure, and the graph is faithful and independent of reduction order. We implemented this operational semantics as a $\lambda$-calculus interpreter. It does dynamic programming automatically, sharing repeated subproblems with no memoization table. It creates and transforms cyclic graphs with no added recursion construct. And it decides in finite time that some terms have no weak head normal form, returning $\bot$ for $\Omega$. What the evaluator returns is a graph, so the $\lambda$-calculus becomes a DSL for graph computation: the memo table of dynamic programming, the transposition table of game search, and the derived-fact table of Datalog reachability and points-to analysis are all tabling on state identity, and none of them is written by hand. Compilation is one more such problem: we write a bootstrap compiler that compiles its own source, all as a pure $\lambda$-term.

papers.title: Memory Layouts for GPU-Data Transfer Buffering in SPH
papers.summary: The rise in GPU compute speed has outpaced improvements in host-to-device memory transfer speeds, despite the advent of shared-memory superchips. Consequently, memory transfer times now constitute an increasingly large fraction of total time-to-solution, compelling developers to compress GPU kernel input and output data into compact, minimal formats prior to GPU-offloading. Complementary to existing work on GPU- and compute-friendly data arrangements, this work argues that significant attention should furthermore be paid to the data organisation on the host such that quick data rearrangements and offloading become feasible. We study a Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics solver and propose memory layout strategies for host-side particle data that are particularly well-suited to GPU-offloading. Specifically, we advocate splitting classic array-of-struct data structures into a struct-of-arrays-of-structs arrangement, in which each logical struct decomposes into substructs determined by kernel read/write access patterns and attribute types. Splitting a monolithic particle struct into several bespoke, finer-grained structs can reduce the time required to pack data to and from buffers by ~20%-40%, lowering total time spent on GPU-offloading by ~12%-25%.

papers.title: Dynamic Load Balancing for Uncertainty Quantification with Applications in Bayesian Inversion
papers.summary: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) workflows present a particular scheduling challenge in high performance computing environments, as they typically generate large numbers of heterogeneous model evaluations with loose but non-trivial dependencies between tasks. A static one-size-fits-all approach in traditional schedulers is inadequate to handle heterogeneous tasks optimally. We introduce an improved load balancer in the UQ and Modelling Bridge (UM-Bridge) framework aimed at mitigating these issues; UM-Bridge is a language-agnostic interface developed to couple UQ software with numerical simulation. This load balancer is first benchmarked against the previous implementation using a synthetic problem. Then, as a realistic example, we test the load balancer with a Bayesian inverse problem solved via multilevel delayed acceptance sampling. The underlying forward problem is a hierarchy of tsunami simulations enabled through ExaHyPE, whose runtimes span several orders of magnitude and loose dependencies between levels make the workload particularly challenging to schedule. Our results indicate the load balancer distributes the sampling requests effectively with an average idle time of close to a millisecond, a thousand times lower than the previous version, without any prior assumptions about the workload or application.

papers.title: Domain Extension of Lock-Freedom and Wait-Freedom for Group Computations
papers.summary: A domain extension of a definition refers to broadening the scope of a definition so that it applies to a larger set of cases than originally specified. The notion of lock-free and wait-free computation is designed for the domain of tasks that are completed by a single thread (in competition with other threads). The goal of this paper is to extend the definition of lock-freedom and wait-freedom to group-computations (denoted by gl-freedom and gw-freedom) that require that the task at hand must be completed by a collaboration between multiple threads. When extending a definition, certain constraints must be respected: the new domain must remain logically consistent with the original meaning, the extension should not introduce contradictions or ambiguities, and it must preserve the essential properties that make the definition valid and useful. We demonstrate this by showing that our extended definition is consistent with the original definition when the group consists of a single thread. We note that extension allows us to characterize programs in a new domain (distributed computing, NUMA computation systems, systems with private data for different threads, etc.) instead of relegating them to be in the same category (deadlock/livelock-free) without regard to the actual properties of that program. We also illustrate this definition with various examples.

papers.title: On the Allocation of Transmit Power for Coordinated Spatial Reuse in IEEE 802.11bn Multi-Access Point Coordination
papers.summary: IEEE 802.11bn (11bn) introduces Coordinated Spatial Reuse (Co-SR), a Multi-Access Point Coordination (MAPC) scheme where two APs coordinate to control the transmit power for a simultaneous transmission. This letter proposes a Proportional Fairness (PF)-driven framework for allocating Co-SR transmit power on a per-Transmission Opportunity (TXOP) basis. We prove that any Pareto-optimal power pair keeps at least one AP at its maximum power, reducing the joint two-dimensional search to two cheap one-dimensional line searches that fit within TXOP timing, and show that this collapses to an exact closed-form expression in a discrete-rate system. We validate these policies and a low-complexity selfish baseline against a brute-force oracle, using packet-level simulations in Kom8ndor, an 11bn simulator. Results show that jointly evaluating both APs' links is key to unlocking Co-SR's gains, that the coordinated AP's fairness-optimal power depends critically on whether the rate is modeled continuously or through discrete Modulation and Coding Scheme (MCS) steps, and that current 11bn signaling supports the selfish policy but not the fairness-optimal ones, which would need additional per-TXOP channel reporting.

papers.title: VeGo: Direct Deductive Formal Verification of Go Programs for Computer Science Education
papers.summary: As formal methods are rapidly becoming accessible and practical due to AI coding agents, priority passes to assisting developers and students in generating specifications. Leveraging native HMX/SSA verifiers provide that support with rigorous mathematical guardrails. We present VeGo (Verified Go), a deductive formal verification system that enables direct verification of standard Go source code. VeGo incorporates Hoare-style contracts, loop invariants and integer variants, well-founded recursive measures, block-level scope invariants, and equational reasoning chains with primed variables directly as non-intrusive Go comments. We detail the language selection rationale justifying Go as an ideal balance over C, C++, Java, and Rust, strategically adopting Go's native multiple return values.
